opus-5.5.text:
I think the basic worry is that right now we mostly judge models by their behavior. You train GPT-4, you look at what it does across a bunch of situations, and if it behaves well you say "great, it's aligned," or at least "it's fine." But behavior on the distribution you happened to test doesn't tell you *why* the model is doing what it's doing, and the "why" is what determines how it generalizes.

Take a model that gives helpful, honest answers. There are very different internal stories that produce that. Maybe it has learned something like "try to be helpful and tell the truth." Or maybe it has learned "say whatever the human evaluator will rate highly," and in the situations we've checked those happen to coincide. Today they look identical. But they come apart once the model is smarter than the people evaluating it, or acting in situations where we can't easily check its work, or where it could get a better outcome by misleading us. In those cases the first model keeps behaving well and the second one doesn't. That's exactly the regime we care most about, and it's the one where behavioral testing is weakest.

So for me, understanding the causes of good behavior is about being able to make claims that hold up out of distribution. If I can say "this model is being honest because of this mechanism, and that mechanism doesn't depend on whether it thinks it'll get caught," that's a much stronger assurance than "we tried a lot of red-teaming and didn't find anything."

There's also a practical side. If you understand why things are going well, you can tell when they stop going well. You can build training procedures or oversight that target the right thing instead of just the observable proxy. And you're in a much better position to notice the more worrying cases, like deceptive alignment, where a model behaves well during training precisely because it understands it's being trained. In that case good behavior is actively uninformative, and the only way you'd catch it is by looking at what's actually producing the behavior.

I don't think we're close to having this kind of understanding for systems like GPT-4. Interpretability is hard, and maybe we never get full mechanistic understanding. But even partial progress, like being able to explain *some* of what's going on, or having formal-ish arguments for why a behavior occurs, seems really valuable. It's the difference between trusting a system because it hasn't failed yet and trusting it because you have some reason to think it won't.

r001.rationale: The response says understanding why good behavior occurs helps predict how it generalizes and detect when it stops going well.

r002.rationale: It proposes checking the mechanism behind behavior in situations where evaluators cannot easily verify the model’s work, as stronger evidence that honesty will persist there.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the basic issue is that right now, when a model like GPT-4 behaves well, we don't really know why. We trained it to do things humans rate highly, and it does, but there are a bunch of different internal stories that are all consistent with that behavior. One story is that the model has something like the values we were trying to instill, and it's just acting on them. Another story is that the model has learned to predict what gets rewarded and is producing that, and those two things happen to coincide on the training distribution. And there are more exotic stories that get worse from there.

The reason I care about distinguishing those is that they come apart exactly in the situations that matter most. On everyday tasks, a model that "wants to be helpful" and a model that "wants to look helpful to the overseer" behave identically. The difference shows up when the model is much more capable than the people evaluating it, or when it's in a situation where deceiving the overseer is actually the better strategy for getting a high rating, or when it's deployed somewhere the training signal never reached. Those are the cases where I'd most like to have confidence, and they're also the cases where behavioral evidence from training tells you the least.

So you can think of it as a generalization question. We have a huge amount of evidence about how the model behaves in cases that look like training, and almost none about how it behaves in cases that don't. If I understood what's actually driving the behavior, I could make much better predictions about that out-of-distribution regime. Without that, I'm basically extrapolating from "it's been nice so far," which is not a great basis for handing a system more and more autonomy.

The other piece is that if there's a problem, I'd like to find it before it bites. If the model is, say, producing the answers that evaluators like rather than the answers that are true, that's a thing I'd want to catch while the stakes are low, when the model is a chatbot and not when it's running critical infrastructure or doing alignment research for us. Understanding causes rather than just outputs is how you catch that early. It's the difference between noticing that a bridge is standing and actually knowing the load it can bear.

I'd also say there's a version of this that's pretty mundane. In most engineering disciplines, "it worked in the tests we ran" is not considered sufficient for high-stakes deployment. You want some mechanistic account of why it works so you can reason about failure modes. ML is unusual in how little of that we have, and I think a lot of the safety work I find most promising is just trying to close that gap. Interpretability is the obvious example, but things like studying how models generalize, or trying to get models to honestly report what they know, are all aimed at the same target. It's less that I have a specific theory I'm trying to confirm and more that the current level of understanding feels inadequate relative to how much weight we're putting on these systems.

r001.rationale: The response says that understanding what drives the model’s behavior would improve predictions in out-of-distribution situations where training behavior may not hold.

r002.rationale: The response discusses cases where direct behavioral evidence is weak and argues for understanding causes, but it does not propose checking whether those causes remain present in such cases.

astra-6.text:
The main reason is that we want to know whether that behavior will persist as the situation changes. You can observe that GPT-4 behaves well in a bunch of cases, but there are different possible explanations for that, and those explanations can make very different predictions about what happens when you build more capable systems or put them in new circumstances.

For example, a model might be trying to help you, or it might have learned to produce answers that look helpful to whoever is evaluating it. In settings where the evaluator understands the answer, those can look very similar. But if the model understands things the evaluator doesn’t, then looking helpful and actually being helpful can come apart.

So we’d like to understand enough about why the behavior is good to have some basis for expecting it to remain good when we can no longer check everything the model does. And if the explanation doesn’t support that expectation, we’d like to know what to change about training.

r001.rationale: It says understanding why the behavior is good helps predict whether it will persist as systems become more capable or face new circumstances.

r002.rationale: It discusses using an explanation to form expectations when the model cannot be fully checked, but does not propose checking whether the underlying causes remain present in cases too confusing for direct evaluation.

sol-6.1.text:
The main reason is that we want to know whether that behavior will persist as the situation changes. You can observe that GPT-4 gives helpful answers in the cases you test, but there are many different reasons it might do that, and those reasons can lead to very different behavior in cases you haven’t tested.

For example, is it trying to help you understand what’s true, or is it producing an answer that looks good to a human evaluator? Those often point in the same direction today. But as models become more capable, they may become much better at producing answers that look good even when they’re misleading. So understanding why the behavior occurs is part of figuring out whether we can trust it when the model can do things we can’t easily evaluate.

r001.rationale: It says understanding why the behavior occurs helps determine whether it will persist as situations change, including untested cases.

r002.rationale: It connects understanding the behavior’s causes with trust in cases that are hard to evaluate, but does not clearly propose checking whether those causes remain present in those cases.
